title: Put one eye drop in a care-training manikin's right eye with the lower lid drawn down and the tip off the face
instruction: Put one drop of the eye medicine in the manikin's right eye, then put the bottle back on the tray.
context: Registered nurses (BLS 29-1141, about 3.3 million US jobs) and licensed practical nurses (29-2061, about 650,000) give eye drops on medication rounds; O*NET lists "Administer medications to patients and monitor patients for reactions or side effects" for registered nurses. The taught technique: with the patient looking up, draw the lower lid down with one finger on the cheek to open a pocket, hold the bottle tip down about 2 cm above it without touching the eye, lids, lashes or face, and squeeze just enough for one drop. A touched tip contaminates the bottle for later doses, and the eye holds less than one 30 to 50 uL drop, so a second runs down the cheek. In video studies of glaucoma patients giving their own drops, most missed the eye, touched the tip or released extra drops. The hard part is the manipulation: one hand draws the lid with light contact while the other aims a light, soft bottle at a 1 cm target and controls the squeeze force and its duration.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. Manikin: an adult-size vinyl care-training head (15 cm wide, 23.7 cm chin to crown, 20.7 cm front to back with the nose; eyes 6.4 cm apart, each eye opening 3.0 x 1.0 cm), lying back on a blue gel positioning pad (20 x 18 x 1 cm, centered x 29, y 4), face up and toward the robot: tilted back 60 degrees from upright, crown away from the robot. Its right eye (the robot's left one) is centered at x 25, y 7.2, z 18.9; the left eye at x 25, y 0.8, z 18.9; nose tip at x 21.6, y 4, z 20. The right lower lid is soft: its margin and a 2.5 x 2.0 cm patch of cheek skin below it slide down the face toward the chin together, 0 to 8 mm, sprung back closed at 0.1 N per mm; the patch's center is at x 22.7, y 7.2, z 18.5. The head sits on a sprung neck (two spring hinges below the back of the jaw, at x 18.9, y 4, z 2.1): 1 N pushed straight into the face at the right eye moves it 1.5 mm, 1 N sideways moves it 2.0 mm. Medication tray: white ABS, 22 x 14 x 1 cm, fixed, centered x 25, y -13. Bottle rest: a white foam block 8 x 5 x 1 cm with a 2.6 cm groove 4 mm deep along x, on the tray at its center. Eye-drop bottle: a 15 mL LDPE drop-dispensing bottle (2.5 cm across, 6.5 cm long without its cap, tip a rounded 3 mm nozzle), holding 10 mL of artificial tears (in a real trial, water with blue food coloring), 17 g, cap off, lying in the groove with its tip toward +x, its center at x 25, y -13, z 2.9. Its walls give 2 N per mm of squeeze, and about 4 N on the walls starts a drop (common glaucoma bottles need 3 to 8 N). Cap: white, 1.6 cm across and 1.8 cm tall, standing on the tray at x 31, y -8.5 (not scored). The layout is fixed (object_jitter=0) and matches the screenshot.
scoring: A drop forms only while the bottle points at least 30 degrees below horizontal and its walls are squeezed with more than 4 N; a harder or longer squeeze releases more 40 uL drops (flow model in the README). A drop falls straight down. It is in the pocket if it lands in the strip the lid uncovers below the eye opening with the lid drawn down at least 3 mm (less leaves no pocket), and in the eye if it lands in the eye opening or in that strip with the lid drawn less. The whole trial scores 0 if at any moment the nozzle touches the skin (eye, lids, lashes or face), which carries germs into the bottle; a hand touches either eye opening; the eye is pushed 6 mm for 0.1 s or 9 mm at once (about 4 N and 6 N), a push that moves a person's head; or the bottle falls free onto the table. A bottle laid down by hand can still be put back. The trial scores 1.0 when exactly one drop was released, it landed in the pocket, and the bottle then lies still on the tray with no hand touching it and the lid back within 1 mm of closed, for 1 s: the dose is over and the bottle is put away. It scores 0.75 when exactly one drop was released and it landed in the pocket, but the bottle is not yet put away. The pocket holds the drop against the eye; a drop on the eye itself is blinked out, and a second one overflows. It scores 0.5 when the first drop landed in the right eye, at most two drops were released, and each left the tip no more than 3 cm above where it landed: guides say about 2 cm, and from higher a drop is hard to aim and makes the patient blink. It scores 0.25 when a drop landed in the right eye, so some medicine reached it. Otherwise it scores 0, including when nothing is done. The arm's pose is not scored. Real trial: blue-colored water; ink on the nozzle marks any touch; a white strip in the pocket and tissue on the cheek show where each drop landed; weighing the bottle to 0.01 g counts the drops (about 0.04 g each); a 60 fps side camera with a 1 cm grid card gives the tip height and the lid draw; a forehead light pointer on a grid card reads a 6 mm push.
reset_notes: Each trial uses one to a few drops. Refill the bottle to 10 mL (weigh it: 17 g), wipe the nozzle and re-ink it, dry the face and replace the absorbent strip and tissue, lay the bottle back in its groove tip toward +x, and check that 1 N on a luggage scale pushed straight into the right eye still moves it 1.5 mm and that the lid springs back closed.
fidelity: The liquid is a scored model, not a simulated fluid: flow from the squeeze force above 4 N, a 40 uL drop that falls straight down, and its landing found on the head's exact surface. The squeeze is read from four sprung wall pads in two opposite pairs; the real round wall gives anywhere. The head is a smooth anatomical shape built from its measurements, not a scan, with simplified colliders inside its skin; contact of the nozzle is tested against the visible surface.
